metadata.title: Gonzales v. Raich, 545 U.S. 1 (2005) (No. 03-1454)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Gonzales v. Raich

Opinion filed: 2005-06-06

Docket No.: 03-1454

Citations:
• 162 L. Ed. 2d 1
• 125 S. Ct. 2195
• 545 U.S. 1
• 2005 U.S. LEXIS 4656

Case holding summaries:
• explaining that marijuana is “a 10 UNITED STATES V. KAPLAN fungible commodity for which there is an established, albeit illegal, interstate market”
• upholding Controlled Substances Act under Commerce Clause without discussion of statute’s jurisdictional element
• recognizing federal law “designates marijuana as contraband for any purpose”
• "The congressional judgment that an exemption for such a sig- nificant segment of the total market would undermine the orderly enforcement of the entire regulatory scheme is entitled to a strong presumption of validity."
• recognizing that it is “of no moment” that Congress’s valid regulation of interstate activity “ensnares some purely intrastate activity”
• explaining that the Necessary and Proper Clause “empowers Congress to enact laws in effectuation of its enumerated powers that are not within its authority to enact in isolation” (emphasis added
• “Our case law firmly establishes Congress’ power to regulate purely local activities that are part of an economic ‘class of activities’ that have a substantial effect on interstate commerce.”
• recognizing federal law “designates marijuana as contraband for any purpose”
• holding that because “Congress had a rational basis” for concluding that a statute implemented Commerce Clause power, the statute fell within the scope of congressional “authority to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper” (quotations omitted)
• upholding statute enacted pursuant to Commerce Clause because “Congress had a rational basis” for concluding that statute implemented congressional power under the Commerce Clause
• recognizing federal law “designates marijuana as contraband for any purpose”
• upholding Congress’s decision to crimi- nalize the production and use of homegrown marijuana even if state law allowed for its growth and use
• Congress has the power to regulate “channels” and “instrumentalities” of interstate commerce even if such regulation “ensnares some purely intrastate activity[.]”
• holding that the federal government had constitutional authority to prohibit and prosecute under federal law the cultivation of marijuana, regardless of whether such activity violated state law
• upholding the ability of the federal government to punish medical marijuana use which is permitted under state law, by virtue of its authority under the Commerce Clause of the United States Constitution
• “‘Economics’ refers to ‘the production, distribution, and consumption of commodities.’”
• distinguishing Morrison because the statute in Raich “directly regulate[d] economic, commercial activity”
• summarizing “considerable efforts,” ultimately unsuccessful, to reschedule marijuana
• recognizing federal law “designates marijuana as contraband for any purpose”
• Congress cannot use "a relatively trivial impact on commerce as an excuse for broad general regulation of state or private activities"
• "[T]hus far in our Nation's history our cases have upheld Commerce Clause regulation of intrastate activity only where that activity is economic in nature" (emphasis added)
• intrastate activities that have been within Congress' power to regulate have been "of an apparent commercial character"
• finding ban on intrastate sale of lighting oils not "appropriate and plainly adapted means for carrying into execution" Congress' taxing power
• "`[W]hen it is necessary in order to prevent an evil to make the law embrace more than the precise thing to be prevented it may do so'"
• discussing the "market value" of marijuana
• activities of a local grain exchange
• finding it "clear, that Congress cannot punish felonies generally," except in areas over which it possesses plenary power
• addressing prescription drugs "for which there is both a lawful and an unlawful market"
• referring to the purchase of drugs on the "retail market"
• "This record leaves us in no doubt" about substantial effects
• "The stimulation of commerce is a use of the regulatory function quite as definitely as prohibitions or restrictions thereon"
• recognizing that Filburn's activity "may not be regarded as commerce"
• "That power can neither be enlarged nor diminished by the exercise or non-exercise of state power"
• recognizing federal law “designates marijuana as contraband for any purpose”
• the Necessary and Proper Clause is "the last, best hope of those who defend ultra vires congressional action"
• "[t]he buying and selling of goods, especially on a large scale, as between cities or nations"
• describing our preference for as-applied rather than facial challenges
• distinguishing the Gun-Free School Zones Act of 1990 from "activities that arise out of or are connected with a commercial transaction"
• "depending on the level of generality, any activity can be looked upon as commercial"
• holding that Congress may regulate the intrastate, noncommercial cultivation, possession, and use of marijuana as an essential part of a larger regulatory scheme
• “[A] primary purpose of the CSA is to control the supply and demand of controlled substances in both lawful and unlawful drug markets.”
• rejecting Commerce Clause challenge to criminalization of home-grown and home-consumed medical marijuana under Controlled Substances Act
• “[Q]uintessentially economic activities [are] the production, distribution, and consumption of commodities for which there is an established, and lucrative, interstate market.”
• explaining that, under the Supremacy Clause, “marijuana possession and cultivation in accordance with state law” is not “beyond congressional reach” (internal quotation marks omitted)
• “Prohibiting the intrastate possession or manufacture of an article of commerce is a rational (and commonly utilized) means of regulating commerce in that product.”
• "We have never required Congress to legislate with scientific exactitude. When Congress decides that the total incidence' of a practice poses a threat to a national market, it may regulate the entire class."
• holding that the regulation of marijuana under the Controlled Substances Act was squarely within Congress's commerce power
• recognizing federal law “designates marijuana as contraband for any purpose”
• reaffirming that federal drug trafficking laws are within Congress's power to regulate interstate commerce
• "[W]hen a general regulatory statute bears a substantial relation to commerce, the de minimis character of individual instances arising under that statute is of no consequence" (internal quotation marks omitted)
